newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania PM says new election law must be passed.
newsitem.headline: Albania PM says new election law must be passed.

text.p: Albanian Prime Minister Bashkim Fino said on Thursday his interim government would resign if parliament did not pass a new law on the voting system to be used in early elections.

The threat exposed cracks in the nine-party National Reconciliation Government set up on March 9 to halt the drift towards anarchy in Albania, where anger over the collapse of pyramid investment schemes had sparked widespread unrest.
Fino told Reuters in an interview that unless the Democratic Party of President Sali Berisha agreed to the new draft law, the government would pass it by majority.

Fino's Socialists and seven other parties in the government want an election with 40 out of the 140 parliamentary seats decided by proportional representation. The Democratic Party wants 115 decided by simple majority.
"I see the danger that this draft passed by the government will pass on to the Albanian parliament where we know that the Democratic Party has the majority," he said.

"A vote against this draft law introduced by the government -- we are speaking of an essential law -- would mean, according to me as prime minister, the fall of the national reconciliation government."

The Democrats won 122 seats in the 140-seat parliament in a general election last May. The Socialists, alleging fraud, withdrew late on polling day. International observers agreed that voting was flawed.
The Socialists won a commitment from Berisha to fresh elections as the price for joining the interim coalition.
Fino said he wanted the eight-nation, Italian-led force now in Albania protecting humanitarian aid deliveries to stay on for the election, due by June 29.
"I would say in reality assistance is necessary ... from the multinational force so that all Albanian polling stations are protected from any kind of problem or incident," Fino said.
The terms of the United Nations mandate for the 6,000-strong force would have to be extended to allow them to help with election security.
Currently, they are meant to secure airports, ports, roads and railways for aid supplies, but not to disarm Albanians or to act as a police force.
Fino acknowledged that widespread looting of military arsenals during the unrest was a long-term problem.

Unofficial estimates say up to a million light weapons, stockpiled by former Stalinist dictator Enver Hoxha to assuage his fears of invasion of his isolationist state, have been distributed among Albania's 3.4 million people.
Several hundred people have been killed, many the victims of accidental or revenge shootings, in the general lawlessness over the past two months.
Fino said the priority should be to collect up heavy weapons.

A brisk trade in the brass casings of artillery shells has sprung up in Europe's poorest nation since the unrest and 27 people were killed when they triggered an explosion while looting an arsenal in central Albania on Wednesday.

Fino said rewards might be offered for citizens to turn in the weapons that had been looted, or the situation could simply be accepted and families encouraged to register the guns they now had in their possession.
"I would say that it will be a problem not simply for the government I head but for future governments," he said.
